To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the geometric structure of eigenvectors of graph Laplacian can be used to design spectral algorithms for graph property testing.
the spectral properties of the graph Laplaican can be used to test if a graph is $(2,\phi)$-clustered and that this can be done with $n^{1/2 + o(1)}$ queries.

(i) the eigenvector of the Laplacian corresponding to the second smallest eigenvalue is the best possible choice for a spectral partitioning algorithm for $(2, \mu \phi)$-clusters, (ii) the spectral norm of the second eigenvector is the right measure for the clusterability of a graph, and (iii) the spectral gap of the graph is the right measure of how close a graph is to being clusterable.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of spectral methods that are applicable to the testing of cluster structure of graphs and we present a new algorithm that is the first to achieve a bound on the query complexity that is sublinear in $n$ for a wide range of parameters.

the following questions. \begin{itemize} \item Can we test clusterability of graphs with a query complexity independent of the size of the graph? \item Can we remove a $\log n \cdot \texttt{poly}(1 / \epsilon, 1 / \phi)$ factor from the query complexity of testing $(k, \epsilon)$-clusterability? \end{itemize}
the development of spectral methods for testing cluster structures in graphs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we present a graph property testing algorithm for the problem of testing cluster structure of a graph.
we present an algorithm with query complexities of $n^{1+o(1)}\epsilon^{O(1)}$ and $\epsilon^{O(2^k)}$ for the cases $k=2, k>2$, respectively.

we provide a spectral method for testing cluster structure in graphs that is faster than the previous spectral method of Chiplunka et al. and that is also faster than the non-spectral method of Czumaj et al.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we provide a unified framework for spectral methods for testing cluster structures of graphs that can be applied to any value of $k$ and that we provide the first algorithm for the case $2 \le k < \infty$ that is independent of the size of the largest cluster.

our algorithm for $k=2$, when $\phi^*$ is small, has a query complexity that is polynomial in $1/\epsilon,1/\phi,\text{poly}(n)$, while the algorithm of Chiplunkkar et al. has a query complexity which is exponential in $1/\phi$.

we provide an alternative algorithm with the same query complexity for the case $ k = 2$ and a different approach for the case of general $k$ that results in an algorithm of query complexity $O\big( n^{k/4+o(1)}\cdot \text{ poly}(\epsilon, k/\phi, \log n)\big)$, improving upon the previous bound of $O(n^k)$.
The main takeaway from our work is that
spectral methods can be used to obtain efficient algorithms for clusterability testing.
spectral properties of a graph can be used to test if the graph admits a cluster partition.
the spectral structure of a graph can be leveraged to obtain algorithms with better query complexity for testing graph properties.
